extracted.intended_audience: legislators, legislative staff, patent practitioners, and stakeholders in patent policy
extracted.subtask_description: Legislative text and Senate floor debate about provisions of patent reform (America Invents Act) including a transitional post-grant review for covered business-method patents and a statutory definition/interpretation of when certain Hatch‑Waxman 60‑day deadlines begin. The page sets procedural, substantive, and policy criteria for those provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establishment of transitional post-grant review program
rubrics_metrics.description: Not later than 1 year after enactment, the Director shall issue regulations establishing and implementing a transitional post-grant review proceeding for review of the validity of covered business-method patents; the proceeding shall be regarded as, and shall employ the standards and procedures of, a post-grant review under chapter 32, subject to specified exceptions and qualifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulations must be issued within 1 year and implement a transitional proceeding for covered business-method patents using post-grant review standards and procedures except where the statute expressly exempts certain post-grant review provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptions to post-grant review provisions for transitional proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 321(c) and subsections (e)(2), (f), and (g) of section 325 shall not apply to a transitional proceeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The transitional proceeding is modeled on post-grant review but explicitly excludes the listed statutory subsections; drafters and regulators must ensure those inapplicable provisions are not applied to transitional proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standing requirement for filing transitional petitions
rubrics_metrics.description: A person may not file a petition for a transitional proceeding with respect to a covered business-method patent unless the person or his real party in interest has been sued for infringement of the patent or has been charged with infringement under that patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transitional petitions are limited to parties who are actual accused infringers or charged, i.e., petitioners must have been sued or charged to seek a transitional review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on grounds for validity challenges (102/103)
rubrics_metrics.description: A petitioner who challenges claims on a ground raised under section 102 or 103 (as in effect on the day prior to enactment) may support such ground only on the basis of: (i) prior art described by section 102(a) (pre-enactment); or (ii) prior art that discloses the invention more than 1 year prior to the patent application date in the United States and would be described by 102(a) if the disclosure had been made by another before the inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Challenges under 102/103 in a transitional proceeding are limited to specific categories of prior art (pre-enactment 102(a) style disclosures or certain >1 year U.S. disclosures); this constrains reliance on other forms of prior art or later statutory formulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estoppel from reasserting grounds after final written decision
rubrics_metrics.description: The petitioner (or his real party in interest) may not assert in a civil action (including actions under section 1338) or in International Trade Commission proceedings that a claim is invalid on any ground that the petitioner raised during a transitional proceeding that resulted in a final written decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A final written decision in a transitional proceeding creates estoppel: grounds raised there cannot later be reasserted in district court or ITC proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Director may institute transitional proceeding only for covered business-method patents
rubrics_metrics.description: The Director may institute a transitional proceeding only for a patent that is a covered business-method patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulations and institution decisions must ensure only patents that meet the statutory covered-business-method definition are subject to transitional review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective date and applicability of regulations
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulations implementing the transitional program take effect 1 year after enactment and apply to all covered business-method patents issued before, on, or after such date, except patents described in section 6(f)(2)(A) during periods where post-grant review petitions would satisfy section 321(c).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The transitional program is broadly applicable across issued patents with specified statutory carve-outs; implementation timing and grandfathering/interaction with other sections must be observed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sunset of the transitional program
rubrics_metrics.description: The subsection establishing the transitional program and its implementing regulations are repealed 4 years after the regulations take effect; however, petitions filed prior to repeal continue to be governed by the regime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The transitional proceeding is temporary (4-year sunset) but will continue to apply to petitions filed before repeal; legislative drafters and stakeholders should account for the temporary nature in strategy and regulatory planning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors for granting a stay of civil infringement actions
rubrics_metrics.description: When a party seeks a stay of a civil action alleging infringement in relation to a transitional proceeding, the court shall decide whether to enter a stay based on: (A) whether a stay will simplify the issues and streamline the trial; (B) whether discovery is complete and whether a trial date has been set; (C) whether a stay would unduly prejudice the nonmoving party or present a clear tactical advantage for the moving party; and (D) whether a stay will reduce the burden of litigation on the parties and on the court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts must weigh these four enumerated factors (simplicity/streamlining, status of discovery/trial scheduling, prejudice/tactical advantage, and burden reduction) in stay decisions; they inform motions practice and litigation strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interlocutory appeal and Federal Circuit review
rubrics_metrics.description: A party may take an immediate interlocutory appeal from a district court's decision on a stay under the transitional proceeding; the Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit shall review the decision to ensure consistent application of established precedent, and such review may be de novo.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stay decisions are immediately appealable to the Federal Circuit, which may review de novo to maintain consistency across courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory definition of 'covered business-method patent'
rubrics_metrics.description: For purposes of the transitional program, a 'covered business-method patent' means a patent that claims a method or corresponding apparatus for performing data processing operations utilized in the practice, administration, or management of a financial product or service, except that the term shall not include patents for technological inventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The definition focuses on data-processing claims tied to financial products/services and expressly excludes 'technological inventions'; regulators must provide criteria to distinguish technological inventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Director's authority to define 'technological invention'
rubrics_metrics.description: Solely for implementing the transitional proceeding, the Director shall prescribe regulations for determining whether a patent is for a technological invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The PTO Director has delegated regulatory authority to create bright-line rules or standards to separate technological inventions from covered business-method patents for administration of the transitional program.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule of construction re: section 101
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing in the transitional program section shall be construed as amending or interpreting categories of patent-eligible subject matter set forth under section 101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The provision does not alter or interpret 35 U.S.C. §101 jurisprudence; patent eligibility law remains governed independently of the transitional program.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniform 'business day' definition for Hatch‑Waxman 60‑day filings (codification of court ruling)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 37 adopts the holding of a district court that when the FDA sends notice of approval after normal business hours, the 60-day filing period for patent term extension begins the next business day; this codifies a 'business day' interpretation to protect applicants from losing statutory time due to bureaucratic timing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statutory change is presented as codifying existing court precedent to ensure uniform treatment across agencies (FDA/PTO) and avoid arbitrary loss of Hatch‑Waxman deadlines due to after-hours transmissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy standard against special congressional relief while litigation is pending
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress should not enact special relief (a private fix) for a party while the matter is still in litigation and on appeal; if relief is warranted after litigation, it should proceed through the special relief procedures with objective justification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Floor debate emphasizes that intervening while appeals are pending undermines the judicial process and that private relief should follow established Congressional special-relief channels after litigation concludes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniformity and equal treatment principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Legislation should ensure uniform definitions (e.g., of 'business day') and consistent application of the law to treat all patent holders equally—preventing bureaucratic inconsistencies from depriving applicants of statutorily granted time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The debate stresses fairness ('equal justice under the law') as a touchstone: statutory language should avoid producing disparate results across jurisdictions or agencies and should protect small/poor litigants as well as large entities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of special-interest bailouts and preservation of legal consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: The Senate floor argument warns against inserting provisions that amount to special favors for wealthy companies or firms (e.g., 'bailout for Medco, WilmerHale') and declares that such ad hoc relief 'corrupts the law'; Congress should not break rules for well‑connected interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy-makers should evaluate provisions for potential special-interest bias and prefer objectively justified, broadly applicable rules implemented through regular procedures rather than case-specific legislative fixes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Codification when courts and agencies agree
rubrics_metrics.description: If a court has ruled and the PTO has adopted that decision, codifying the court's interpretation into statute (e.g., how to count days for patent-term extension) is appropriate to provide certainty and avoid further confusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The floor text argues that when judicial decisions resolve ambiguity and the agency follows, statutory codification can 'put the issue to bed' and provide certainty for stakeholders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of economic and consumer impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: Provisions like section 37 are characterized as budget-neutral and 'not anticonsumer'; the legislative rationale includes assertions that the change supports medical innovation, patient access, and does not impose net costs on taxpayers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislative justifications should address budgetary neutrality and consumer impacts (e.g., effect on medical research and patient access) when defending technical patent rules.
